Growth Mixture Parameter Estimates with Standard Errors

Source: R/gmm_se.R
growth_estimates.Rd

Returns every parameter of a fit_gmm() fit – the growth-factor means (intercepts, when there are growth_predictors), the growth-factor regressions, the growth-factor variances and covariances, the residual variances, the fitted trajectory and the class-size logits – with a standard error, a z statistic and a two-sided p-value.

Usage

growth_estimates(fit, se = c("robust", "hessian", "opg"))

Arguments

fit

A model returned by fit_gmm().

se

Which standard-error estimator: "robust" (default), "hessian" or "opg". See Details.

Value

A data frame with one row per parameter and class: parameter ("growth_mean", "growth_regression", "growth_variance", "growth_covariance", "residual_variance", "fitted" or "class_logit"), item, class, estimate, se, z and p_value. The covariance matrix of the reported parameters is attached as the attribute "vcov".

Details

The standard errors are computed from the log-likelihood of the fitted model itself, by differentiating it with respect to the parameters the fit estimated, and are then carried to the reported scale by the delta method. Three estimators are offered:

  • "robust" (the default) is the sandwich \(H^{-1} B H^{-1}\), where \(H\) is the observed information (minus the matrix of second derivatives of the log-likelihood) and \(B\) the sum over cases of the outer product of each case's score (White, 1982). It stays a valid variance when the within-class normal model is only approximately right, which for a growth mixture is the usual situation: the classes are partly a device for describing a non-normal distribution of trajectories (Bauer & Curran, 2003).

  • "hessian" is \(H^{-1}\), the inverse observed information, the textbook maximum-likelihood variance when the model is correct.

  • "opg" is \(B^{-1}\), the inverse outer product of the case scores, which estimates the same quantity as "hessian" under a correct model from first derivatives alone.

When the model is right the three agree in large samples; a marked gap between "robust" and the other two is a sign of misspecification. With sample weights every case's contribution is weighted, and with a cluster variable the scores are summed within clusters before \(B\) is formed.

Constrained parameters are repeated across the classes they are shared by, with the same standard error, as in measurement_summary(). The prior that keeps the variances away from zero during estimation is not part of the variance: these are the standard errors of the likelihood.

A growth-factor covariance matrix outside the positive semi-definite cone still gets standard errors (see psi in fit_gmm()); the point is a maximum of the likelihood like any other. Where the information matrix is singular – a parameter the data do not identify – the standard errors are NA and a warning says so.

The class-size logits are \(\log(\pi_k / \pi_K)\). When the class sizes are modelled by predictors they are not reported here; see coef(). Under n_steps = 3 the standard errors here are those of the step-1 model, which is where the growth parameters are estimated.

References

White, H. (1982). Maximum likelihood estimation of misspecified models. Econometrica, 50(1), 1-25. doi:10.2307/1912526

Louis, T. A. (1982). Finding the observed information matrix when using the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 44(2), 226-233. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1982.tb01203.x

Bauer, D. J., & Curran, P. J. (2003). Distributional assumptions of growth mixture models: Implications for overextraction of latent trajectory classes. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 338-363. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.338

See also

fit_gmm(), measurement_summary().

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
n <- 400
cls <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
icept <- ifelse(cls == 1, 3, 1) + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
slope <- ifelse(cls == 1, 1.0, 0.2) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)
y <- outer(icept, rep(1, 4)) + outer(slope, 0:3) + matrix(rnorm(n * 4, 0, 0.7), n, 4)
fit <- fit_gmm(y, times = 4, n_classes = 2, n_init = 10, random_state = 1)
growth_estimates(fit)
